This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term> <note>A legal status where a work is no longer protected by copyright law, allowing anyone to use it freely.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia</term> <note>Handwritten notes, sketches, or comments made by previous readers in the margins of a book's pages.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying <note>This refers to the use of software scripts or "bots" to download large amounts of data automatically.</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.
+ **Maintain attribution** The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at <insert>http://books.google.com/</insert>

## **About this book**

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before being digitized by Google as part of a project aimed at making the world’s books available online.

It has survived long enough to no longer be protected by copyright and has entered the **public domain**. The classification of a book as being in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are the link to our past, representing a heritage of history, culture, and knowledge that is often difficult to discover.

## **Usage guidelines**

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them universally available. Public domain books belong to the public, and we are merely their custodians. However, this work is costly; therefore, to continue offering this service, we have taken certain initiatives to prevent illicit use by commercial entities, including the imposition of restrictions on the submission of automated queries <note>The use of software scripts or "bots" to search or download data automatically without human intervention.</note>.

Furthermore, we ask that you:

+ *Do not make commercial use of these files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individual private users, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Do not send automated queries* Do not send automated queries of any kind to Google. If you are conducting research in the field of machine translation, optical character recognition (<term>OCR</term> <note>Technology that converts images of typed, handwritten, or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note>), or other fields where you need to use large amounts of text, we invite you to contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain the watermark* The Google "watermark" that appears in each file is essential for informing users about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Do not remove it.

+ *Use it legally* Regardless of how you use it, remember that it is your responsibility to ensure you are doing so legally. Do not assume that because a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, it is also in the public domain for users in other countries. The criteria determining whether a book is protected by copyright vary from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether a specific use of the book is permitted. Do not assume that because a book appears in Google Book Search, it means it can be used in any way and in any country in the world. Penalties for copyright violations can be very severe.

# NOTICE TO THE READERS

---

**I**T SEEMS that to those monks, who were granted by *Providence* <note>Divine guidance or care.</note> the task of rescuing the works of human genius from the malice of barbarian centuries, has been entrusted the noble duty of making them public property for the advancement of human knowledge. Modern civilization, which desires such a duty to be fulfilled especially by those of *Monte Cassino* <note>The Abbey of Monte Cassino, established in 529 AD, is one of the most famous monasteries in the world and a historical center for the preservation of Latin and Greek texts.</note>, as the guardians of a most distinguished *Archive* <note>The abbey’s archive is one of the world's most significant, containing over 40,000 parchments and thousands of manuscripts.</note>, would raise a just complaint against them if, amidst such literary wealth, they were to lounge in idleness and not decide to gift others some unknown writing useful to either the mind or the heart. Nor did the Cassinese <note>The monks of the Monte Cassino community.</note> forget such a holy duty. In the last century, to speak of times less distant from our age, *Gattola* <note>Erasmo Gattola (1662–1734), a monk and historian at Monte Cassino whose monumental works are foundational for the abbey's history.</note> wrote...

<term>Notice to the readers<gloss>Italian: "Avviso ai leggitori." A standard preface in historical books where the author or editor explains the purpose and origin of the work.</gloss></term>
<term>Providence<gloss>Italian: "Provvidenza." A reference to God's intervention in human history, often invoked by religious writers to explain the survival of ancient texts.</gloss></term>
<term>Monte Cassino<gloss>The mother house of the Benedictine Order, located in Italy.</gloss></term>
<term>Archive<gloss>Italian: "Archivio." Refers specifically to the vast collection of historical documents and codices held by the monastery.</gloss></term>
<term>Gattola<gloss>Referring to Dom Erasmo Gattola, the most prominent historian of the Cassinese community.</gloss></term>
<term>Cassinese<gloss>Italian: "Cassinesi." A term used for the monks of Monte Cassino.</gloss></term>

<summary>This preface introduces the monks of Monte Cassino as the providential guardians of human knowledge, justifying the publication of this work as a fulfillment of their duty to share their archival treasures with the modern world.</summary>
<keywords>Monte Cassino, Benedictine monks, archival preservation, Erasmo Gattola, cultural heritage, scholarship</keywords>

-># NOTICE<-

...wrote the History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino, and Father Federici <note>Domenico Federici (1739–1808), a scholar who worked on the diplomatic history of Gaeta.</note> wrote that of the *Hypati* of Gaeta <note>Hypati (Ipati) was a Byzantine title for high-ranking officials or consuls who governed Gaeta.</note>; and both, by producing Bulls, Diplomas, and other records, rescued these from oblivion and increasingly brought human events to light. Through the work of Father Fraja <note>Don Angelo Maria Fraja, a monk and archivist at Monte Cassino.</note>, prefect of the Cassinese Archive, ten Sermons of *St. Augustine* <note>A foundational Father of the Church (354–430 AD).</note> saw the light for the first time in our day, and he deserved well of the *republic of letters* <note>The "Republic of Letters" was the long-distance intellectual community in the 17th and 18th centuries that fostered the exchange of ideas.</note>. The upheaval to which Europe was subjected, the voice of a century that *cries "crucify them"* <note>original: "grida la croce"—an allusion to the biblical "Crucify Him," referring here to the intense anti-clerical and anti-monastic movements of the late 18th and early 19th centuries.</note> against monastic orders, if it discouraged the spirit of the Cassinese from literary undertakings, it did not degrade them; and the talent for helping others, of not remaining useless members of society, and the memory of having been the conservators of *Wisdom*, still makes them promoters of it today.

Even those least knowledgeable in Italian matters are aware of the Cassinese Archive, and of the wealth of manuscripts preserved within it, and of the many things which remain unknown and which would be useful to publish. Among the seven hundred Codices <note>Handwritten books, particularly ancient ones.</note>, either written by the hands of the monks or through their care...

<term>Hypati<gloss>From the Greek "hypatos," meaning consul; a title used by the rulers of Gaeta during the period of Byzantine influence.</gloss></term>
<term>Republic of letters<gloss>Italian: "repubblica letteraria." A term used to describe the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</gloss></term>
<term>Codices<gloss>Plural of codex; ancient manuscript books, often of vellum or parchment, which replaced the scroll format.</gloss></term>

-># TO THE READERS<-

---

...collected, there is a paper one from the **14th** century, in which one reads the Vernacular Translation <note>A "volgarizzamento" is a translation from Latin into the common "vulgar" tongue (Italian), making scholarly works accessible to the general public during the Renaissance.</note> by Master Donato di Casentino of the work by Master Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous Italian author and poet, best known for the *Decameron*.</note>, titled *On Famous Women* <note>original: *De Claris Mulieribus*</note>. An index of the Chapters and a brief Prologue by the same Donato precede the *Lives* by Boccaccio in this Codex <note>A "codex" refers to a manuscript in book form rather than a scroll.</note>. I will mention this and other translators, following what has been written by Argelati <note>Filippo Argelati (1685–1755), an Italian bibliographer who documented the history of Italian writers.</note> and Villa <note>Ignazio Villa, an 18th-century scholar who provided commentary and notes on Boccaccio’s texts.</note>, the latter of whom provided the notes to his work.

-># TO THE READERS<-

*Now that Italian minds have returned to the purity of their own language—which had been sullied and bastardized by foreign ways during the time when not only bodies but minds, and even speech itself, had to groan under the transalpine yoke <note>A reference to French political and linguistic influence in Italy, particularly during the Napoleonic era.</note>—we believe we are performing a useful service for our fatherland by producing a text which, like a hidden treasure of many beauties, is rich in its command of the language. Indeed, it abounds in elegant expressions that are sought after even in the <term>Crusca Vocabulary</term> <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca*, first published in 1612, was the primary authority on the "pure" Italian language based on 14th-century Florentine standards.</note> itself.*

*Therefore, let the readers not believe that this translation by <term>Master Donato</term> is one of those 14th-century scrapbooks <note>original: "scartabelli del Trecento"</note> which offer you very little gold and much dross; rather, it is a source of rare beauty, which we bestow upon those who dedicate themselves to the Italian tongue and are protective of its purity.*

*We hope that readers will not wish to blame us for too much boldness if the archaic spelling of the <term>Codex</term> has been adapted to modern fashion, in such a way that there is no change of any kind in the words or the meaning. And since in our copy there is no punctuation whatsoever to divide sentences and distinguish one sense from another, we supplied this lack not according to our own whims, but as the Latin text of <term>Boccaccio</term> <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), author of the *Decameron*. This suggests the manuscript is an early Italian translation of one of Boccaccio's Latin works.</note> required.*

*May the readers look favorably upon this work of ours, printed for their benefit, and to clarify to others that the* <term>Cassinese</term> <note>The Benedictine monks of Monte Cassino, an abbey famous as a center of medieval learning and manuscript production.</note> *have not ceased their industriousness in studies, being mindful of the glory that the wisdom of the ancient* **Monks** *of* **Monte Cassino** *brought to our country.*

# HISTORICAL MEMOIRS

## ON THE LIFE

### OF MASTER DONATO DA CASENTINO.

## BY THE EDITOR

**P**ERHAPS some will wonder that I passed over in silence, in the brief *Notice to the Readers*, the person of Master Donato da Casentino <note>Donato degli Albanzani (c. 1326–1411), known as Donato da Casentino, was a famous humanist, a friend of Petrarch, and the translator of Boccaccio's Latin works into the Italian vernacular.</note>, the author of this valuable book; and perhaps in their thoughts they might have deemed me lazy or ignorant. But if I remained silent concerning his life, it was from a desire to offer in a separate discourse whatever I might manage to discover in other books regarding the Life and Works of Master Donato. And here is the fruit of my labors—if small, it is not useless.

The fourteenth century <note>The 1300s, a period marked by both the early stirrings of the Renaissance and significant political turmoil across the Italian peninsula.</note> was underway: and although this poor land of Italy was troubled by

Dante’s ashes were still warm: and, as if from sparks awakened by them, the minds of Petrarch, Boccaccio, and others were forged, bringing further fame to the land that had produced them. Donato da Casentino raised a more brilliant reputation for himself, both through the works that proclaim him a master of polished speech <term>Polished speech: This refers to "forbita favella," the elegant and refined use of the Italian vernacular which was becoming a literary standard at the time.</term>, and through the friendship that sweetly united him to Petrarch, Boccaccio, and other illustrious men of letters.

Master Donato was almost always called "Apennine-born" <gloss>(1)</gloss> <note>original: "Appenninigena."</note> by Petrarch, and the Abbot Mehus also gives him the surname Albanzani <gloss>(2)</gloss>. If the first name comes from Donato having been born near the Apennine mountains, where the province of Casentino <note>A valley in eastern Tuscany known for its natural beauty and historical importance.</note> lies, we cannot agree with Tiraboschi <note>Girolamo Tiraboschi (1731–1794), a Jesuit priest and famous historian of Italian literature.</note> that Mehus gave Donato the second name without evidence. For Mehus <gloss>(3)</gloss>, when listing the names of those to whom Coluccio Salutato <note>A political and cultural leader in Florence, one of the most important figures of the early Renaissance.</note> addressed his letters, gives the surname Albanzani to Donato, having read it in the codices <term>Codices: Handwritten manuscript books, the precursor to the modern printed book.</term> in which Coluccio's letters were written. Certainly Donato was born in Pratovecchio, a town in the Casentino, because Petrarch, speaking of him in his will, says: *To Master Donato of Pratovecchio* <note>original Latin: "Magistro Donato de Prato veteri."</note>: but

### HISTORICAL MEMOIRS ON HIS LIFE

->page 18<-

It is no easy thing to discover in which year he was born. It is true, however, that from the following words in the letter that Petrarch chose to address to him to temper the bitter grief he felt over the death of a son named Solone, it is clearly shown that Donato was not born before 1330. *It is said that Augustus placed a consecrated image in his bedchamber of his great-grandson, who died at the same age as your son.* <note>original Latin: "Augustus pronepotuli sui, hac Aetate qua filius tuus erat extincti imaginem in cubiculo suo consecratam posuisse traditur."</note> Solone died <gloss>(1)</gloss> in the year 1368, the year in which Petrarch consoled him with this letter; and having lived eighteen years, like the grandson <note>The Latin quote mentions a "great-grandson," but the author here likely refers to Marcellus, the nephew of Augustus, who died young and was famously mourned.</note> of Augustus, he came into the world in 1350. Therefore Donato, having fathered him at the age of at least twenty years, could have been born around the year 1330 or 1336.

Because Donato was a man to be honored for his knowledge, many famous figures of that century desired his friendship and studied to cultivate it. For, as poor as he was, according to Boccaccio <gloss>(2)</gloss>, and not yet having entered the court of Ferrara <note>The House of Este in Ferrara was a major center for arts and scholarship where Donato would eventually find patronage.</note>, nor enjoying wealth or favor—

Among Italian cities, Venice was also adorned with a distinguished university: Donato was summoned there to serve as a master of grammar <note>In the 14th century, a "master of grammar" was not just a language teacher, but a professor of Latin literature and the humanities.</note>. ->## BY MASTER DONATO DA CASENTINO.<-

While Donato lived in this city devoting himself to public instruction, he received many letters from Petrarch, in which the latter, in a certain way, poured out his whole heart; it is a pleasure to read them today to understand the deep affection these two talented men of letters shared for one another.

Among the others, a very beautiful proof of their friendship is the letter Petrarch wrote to him to offer comfort after the death of Donato's son, Solon. This tragedy was soon followed by the loss of the only son remaining to him, Antonio. In this correspondence, Coluccio seeks his friendship and makes him aware of his own great desire to associate with him through letters, because he had heard Donato spoken of as a most wise man (1).

# PREFACE
## BY MASTER BOCCACCIO <note>original: "M. Boccaccio". M. stands for Messer, a title of respect equivalent to Master or Sir.</note>
### TO THE READERS
->TRANSLATED INTO THE VERNACULAR BY BETUSSI<- <note>original: "volgarizzato". This refers to the act of translating the original Latin text into the Italian "volgare" or common tongue so it could be read by a wider audience.</note>

**S**OME ancients wrote short books a long time ago concerning illustrious men, and at present, with a sharper style and more at length, the famous man and excellent poet **Francesco Petrarca** <note>A renowned Italian scholar and poet (1304–1374), often considered the father of Humanism.</note> our teacher <note>Boccaccio held Petrarch in high esteem, viewing him as a mentor and intellectual father.</note>, is worthily producing a volume on them; for truly those who applied every diligence, their resources, their blood, and their soul—according to the needs of the time—to surpass others through virtuous works, have deserved that their names be held in perpetual remembrance by their successors. 

But I have wondered greatly that women have had so little standing alongside such men, such that they have not obtained any favor of memory in any specific account <note>Boccaccio is observing that while there are many collections of biographies for "illustrious men," there was a lack of similar books dedicated to women.</note>; for it is clearly seen through the most extensive histories that many women have conducted themselves with as much valor as they have with strength. And if men are to be exalted, who, having been given natural strength, have performed worthy deeds, how much more so should women be, to almost all of whom by... <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

# PREFACE

*...by nature they are given a delicacy, a weak body, and a slow intellect; yet if they acquire a generous spirit and a sharp mind, and with notable virtue dare to execute difficult and nearly impossible things, do they not deserve to be held in high esteem? Therefore, so that they are not cheated of their rightful merit, it came into my mind to create a memorial in honor of those who can be remembered, and to bring them together. To these, I am adding a few of the many whom boldness, or strength, and industriousness of intellect, or a gift of nature, or the grace of fortune—or even some injury—has made notable. I am not leaving behind any woman who, although she performed no deed worthy of memory herself, nonetheless provided great occasions so that others, by her means, performed notable actions worthy of remembrance.* <note>Boccaccio suggests that even women who were passive "muses" or causes of great events deserve inclusion alongside active heroines.</note> *Nor do I want it to seem improper to the reader if he finds—alongside **Penelope**, **Lucrezia**, and **Sulpizia**, who were most chaste women—the likes of **Medea**, **Flora**, and **Sempronia**, who possessed very great but most wicked intellects.* <note>**Penelope** (wife of Odysseus) and **Lucretia** (Roman matron) were traditional symbols of virtue. **Medea** (the sorceress) and **Sempronia** (involved in the Catilinarian conspiracy) represent the "illustrious" through infamy rather than purity.</note> *For it is not my intention to take this name of "noble" and "illustrious" in such a narrow sense that it always seems to result in virtue; rather, with the readers' kind permission, I intend to apply it in a broader sense: understanding as "illustrious" those whom I recognize as most famous and well-known through any deed made public to the world. I recall having often read, among the likes of **Leonidas**, the **Scipios**, the **Catoc**, and the **Fabricii**...* <note>These are famous Greek and Roman male leaders and heroes typically featured in the "Illustrious Men" books Boccaccio is emulating.</note>

<summary>Boccaccio explains his criteria for including women in his book, arguing that "illustrious" refers to renown and impact (whether virtuous or wicked) rather than moral perfection alone.</summary>
<keywords>Boccaccio, Famous Women, virtue vs. notoriety, Penelope, Medea, Scipio, Lucretia, gender roles in history</keywords>

->BY MESSER BOCCACCIO.<-

...illustrious men, such as the most seditious **Gracchi**, the astute *Hannibal*, the traitor *Jugurtha*, those stained with the blood of civil war *Sulla* and *Marius*, the rich and greedy *Crassus*, and others of their kind. <note>Boccaccio lists famous figures from Roman and Carthaginian history who were "illustrious" for their power or infamy rather than their moral goodness. The **Gracchi** were brothers and controversial reformers; **Jugurtha** was a North African king who fought Rome; **Sulla** and **Marius** were rivals in a bloody civil war.</note> Besides, if I had raised up with praise those worthy of memory and brought down with rebukes those who were shameful, it would not only have brought no small glory to the noble and no small infamy to the wicked; it would also have seemed that I had strayed little from the usual path, or rather that I had wished to renew those accounts that seem to have faded through the long passage of time. I have also thought it right at times to include among these histories some kind examples and virtuous exhortations, adding to them, by contrast, sharp motivations to flee and avoid wicked deeds; for by joining pleasure with history, the mind gains greater benefit. <note>This follows the classical literary theory that writing should both "teach and delight."</note> And so that it does not seem—according to ancient custom—that I have only touched upon the surface <term>principj (principles)</term> <note>original: "principj," referring here to the basic outlines or summaries of the stories.</note> of these matters which I have found in the works of trustworthy authors, I have expanded them into a fuller and longer history. I consider it not only useful but necessary that these works should please men no less than women; for while women are generally less familiar with history, they have a greater need for it and take more joy in a detailed narrative. It will also appear that I have perhaps forgotten—excepting *Eve*, our first mother...

<meta>This page continues the Preface of Boccaccio’s "Concerning Famous Women" (De Mulieribus Claris), translated into Italian by Giuseppe Betussi. Boccaccio is explaining his editorial choice to exclude Biblical and Christian figures from this specific collection, focusing instead on the "Gentile" (Pagan) women of antiquity.</meta>

->PREFACE BY MESSER BOCCACCIO.<-

...of all, [it may be asked why] among all these **Pagan** women I have not included any Hebrew or Christian woman. <note>original: "Gentili." In this context, Boccaccio refers to the women of Greek, Roman, and other non-Abrahamic civilizations.</note> But I have refrained, because it did not seem to me that they belong well together, nor that they desired to reach the same goal in equal measure. For the former <note>The Hebrew and Christian women.</note> truly strove for the sake of true and eternal glory, very often forcing themselves to overcome adversity and human miseries by imitating the sacred and holy commandments; whereas the latter <note>The Pagan women.</note>, either through a certain gift of nature or rather moved by a desire for such sudden splendor—though not without great strength of mind—attained a name for eternity, many times enduring the greatest misfortunes and infinite assaults of *Fortune*. <note>Boccaccio highlights a distinction between religious "virtue" (aimed at Heaven) and secular "fame" (aimed at historical immortality).</note>

Beyond this, those holy women not only live most clearly and resplendently in the true and eternal light of their deserved immortality, but we know their virginity, chastity, holiness, and virtue—both in conquering the <term>concupiscence (carnal desire)</term> of the flesh and the torments of tyrants—and their invincible constancy, to have been described in more than one volume by many holy men most learned in the sacred scriptures and greatly honored. And therefore, I have not wished to compare any of their merits, as they have been written by others, with these women [of this book], for their merits are far greater than those of the figures I now strive to write about in order to grant them some reward. May God, Father of all, be present at this pious work and grant favor to what I am about to write, allowing me to write it for His true praise.

<summary>Boccaccio concludes his preface by explaining that he has excluded Christian and Hebrew women because their spiritual achievements are too superior to be compared with the secular fame of Pagan women, and their lives are already well-documented by Church fathers.</summary>

# CHAPTER ONE

## Concerning Eve.

**S**ince I must write about the virtues for which famous women are known, it will not seem an unworthy thing to take the beginning from she who was the mother of all men: Eve. She was, without a doubt, the first mother, and was glorious with magnificent virtues; for she was not produced in this laborious valley of miseries <note>A common medieval metaphor for the mortal world after the Fall.</note> in which all we other men are born to toil, nor was she fabricated with that hammer or with that anvil <note>Metaphorical language referring to natural human procreation.</note> as others are in this life, into which she did not enter weak and weeping for the sin of her nature as others do. 

Instead, the excellent Creator <note>original: "Fattore" – literally the Maker or Doer.</note> of all things, having formed Adam with His own hand from the mud of the earth—a thing which has not happened to any other person since—and having placed him in the Garden of Delights <note>The Garden of Eden.</note>, which was later called the Field of Damascus <note>A medieval tradition suggested that Adam was created in a place called the "Ager Damascenus" (the Field of Damascus) before being placed in Eden.</note>, and having made him fall into a pleasant sleep; by a skill known only to Him, He drew her from the side of that sleep-

# CHAPTER I.

### CHAPTER I.

...fully formed, and she was in her husband's company, joyful at the sight of that delightful place; and He made her the immortal mistress of all things alongside the man, who was now awake, and by him she was even called Eve. And what greater or more glorious thing could ever happen to anyone at their birth? Furthermore, we may consider her to have been marvelous for the beauty of her body; for nothing is made by the hand of God that does not surpass others in beauty. ## CHAPTER V.

->*Ceres, Goddess of Grain, Queen of Sicily.*<-

**CERES**, as many are pleased to believe, was a most ancient queen of Sicily. She possessed such great intellect that, having devised the cultivation of the soil, she was the first among her people to tame oxen and invent the plow and the plowshare <term>plowshare: the main cutting blade of a plow that carves the furrow</term>. She taught the oxen to bear the yoke and, through their labor, to cleave the earth and scatter seed in the furrows. As this grew into an abundance of grain, she taught men—who were accustomed to living on acorns and fruit—how to extract it from the ears of grain, grind the grain, leaven the flour, and give it substance <note>The original "farne corpo" literally means "to give it body," referring to the process of making bread.</note>. Because of this service, although she was a mortal woman, those people thought her to be the Goddess of Grain, honoring her with divine gifts; and it was believed that she was (1) born of Saturn and Cybele.

---

(1) The Cassinese Codex reads: "and it was believed she was born of Saturn, etc." <note>original: "e fu creduto chella generata di Saturno, ecc."</note>.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### Isis, Queen of Egypt.

Isis, who was previously called **Io**, was not only the queen of the Egyptians, but eventually became their most holy and venerable Goddess. Nevertheless, there was doubt among the ancient writers of history regarding her parentage and the time in which she was born. There were some who said that she was the daughter of Inachus, the first king of the Argives <note>Inhabitants of the Greek city-state of Argos.</note>, and the sister of Phoroneus; it is clear that they reigned during the time of **Jacob**, the son of **Isaac** <note>This reflects a common medieval practice of synchronizing Greek mythology with Biblical history.</note>. Others affirm that she was the daughter of Prometheus, while **Phorbas** was the lord of Argos, which was much later than the first period mentioned. Some claim she lived during the time of **Cecrops**, king of the Athenians; and some say she was in the time of **Lycaeus**, king of the Argives: such variations among learned men are not without reason. All affirm that she was, among the other women of her time, noble and most worthy of remembrance (1). Truly she—

## CHAPTER X.

### *Libya, Queen of Libya.*

**LIBYA**, according to what the ancient writers say, was the daughter of Epaphus, King of Egypt, and Cassiopeia his wife. She was the wife of Neptune, a powerful foreigner whose real name has not survived to our day; with him, she gave birth to Busiris <note>In Greek mythology, Busiris was a king of Egypt who sacrificed visitors to the gods to end a famine; here, the author treats him as a historical tyrant.</note>, the cruel tyrant of Upper Egypt. However, her magnificent works have been consumed by time. It is a strong argument for her greatness that she held such authority among her people that the entire part of Africa over which she reigned has been called Libya after her name. <note>In ancient geography, "Libya" was often used as a name for the entire continent of Africa, or specifically the regions west of the Nile.</note>

### NIOBE, CHAPTER XIV.

Therefore, she should have offered thanks—as was her duty—to the one God for the children she was granted, rather than demanding divine honors for herself, as if having such a great number of wonderful children had been her own achievement. Because she acted with pride rather than wisdom, she spent her life weeping for her misfortune; and many centuries later, her name remains hateful to those who come after her.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## *Arachne of Asia.*

**Arachne** was a woman of Asia, and was of the common people, the daughter of Idmon of Colophon, a dyer of wool; who, although she was not famous for her lineage, nevertheless ought to be celebrated for certain of her virtues. Some ancient writers claim that she discovered the use of flax, and that she was the first to conceive of making nets: it is uncertain whether they were for fishing or for fowling <note>The hunting or trapping of birds.</note>. And since her son, who was named Closter <note>The name is derived from the Greek word "kloster," meaning spinner.</note>, had invented spindles suitable for the craft of wool-working (1), they believe that she held the pre-eminence in the art of weaving, and that she was of great genius; for with her fingers, with the threads and with the shuttle, and with the other tools suited to such tasks, she worked that which the painter did with the brush; and this artistry is not to be despised in a woman. And certainly, hearing such clear renown not only in Colophon—

## ***Deianira, Wife of Hercules.***

**Deianira**, according to what some affirm, was the daughter of Oeneus, king of Aetolia, and the sister of Meleager; and she was famous for such great beauty that Hercules and Achelous <note>A river god capable of changing into various shapes, including a bull, to fight Hercules.</note> fought to have her as a wife. Having remained with Hercules <note>Meaning Hercules won her in the contest.</note>, she was loved by Nessus the Centaur. And as Hercules was carrying her from Calydon to his own country, he was held back by the Evenus (1), a river of Calydon, which had swollen due to rain. There, the enamored Nessus came to meet him; because he was part horse (2), he offered to serve Hercules by carrying Deianira across the river. After Hercules had given his wife to him, and as he prepared to swim across, Nessus—becoming content in his desire and having already crossed the river—began to flee with his prey. And since Hercules could not follow him on foot, he struck him with an arrow poisoned with Lernaean blood <note>The venomous blood of the Hydra of Lerna, which Hercules had killed during his Second Labor.</note>. ### CHAPTER XXIV.

[She came to] Rome to **Tarquin the Elder** <note>original: "Tarquinio Prisco" — the legendary fifth king of Rome who reigned in the 6th century BCE</note>, and brought him nine books, of which she burned three in his presence, as he was unwilling to give her the price she demanded for them; and the following day she asked him for that same price she had previously wanted for all nine, asserting to him that if he did not give it to her immediately, she would burn three more, and on the following day the remaining three; at which point he paid the requested price. These books, preserved thereafter, were found to contain all the destinies and struggles of the Romans. For this reason, the Romans later kept them with great diligence, and according to the necessity of seeking counsel regarding future events, they would hasten to them as if to a temple.

### CHAPTER XXV.

Spaniards, nor the barbarians of any other stock with their assault: so that they never said, nor dared to say, that by their own merit the first letters were discovered; and much less that they discovered the rules of grammar; which, just as we discovered them, so we gave them to those peoples, forever marked with our own Latin terms. 

From this it follows that the further these letters are carried abroad, the more the praises and honors of the Latin name are magnified. They bear a clearer witness to our ancient honor, nobility, and genius; and they preserve an uncorrupted proof of our intellectual <term>subtlety</term> <note>original: "sottilità"; referring here to the refined sharpness of the Roman mind in creating complex systems like grammar</note>, even despite the shameful actions of the barbarians. For this singular glory, although we must give thanks to God who granted these gifts, we are nonetheless bound to <term>Carmenta</term> <note>Also known as Nicostrata, she was a prophetic goddess or princess credited in mythology with adapting the Greek alphabet into the Latin one</note> with great praise, affection, and devotion. It is therefore a dutiful thing that we honor her greatness as much as we are able in eternal memory, so that we are not judged as ungrateful by those who come after us.

# CHAPTER XXIX.

## *Regarding the Wives of Jason’s Companions.*

We do not know the number, nor the names, of the wives of the <term>Minyans</term> <note>original: "Menj"; an ancient Greek group, many of whom were Argonauts</note>; whether this is due to the laziness of those who wrote in their own time, or due to the fault of the long passage of years, it is a shameful thing; for these women earned the greatest praise and glory for their great deeds. But since it has so pleased hateful Fortune, I shall strive with as much skill as I can to restore those who are named, to the best of my power, with worthy praise to the memory of those who will come after, as they are those who have well deserved it. 

The <term>Minyans</term>, then, were the companions of <term>Jason</term> <note>the mythological hero who led the quest for the Golden Fleece</note> and were among the <term>Argonauts</term> <note>the heroes who sailed aboard the ship *Argo*</note>—famous young men of no small nobility. When their journey to <term>Colchis</term> <note>original: "Colco"; an ancient region on the Black Sea coast where the Golden Fleece was kept</note> was completed and they had returned to Greece, they left their ancient homeland and chose to establish their seat among the <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>the Spartans</note>. By these people, not only was citizenship kindly granted to them, but they were even received among the Senators who governed the Republic. However, the successors of the Spartans, not being mindful of this splendid courtesy, dared— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ardi-", likely leading into "ardirono" (they dared) on the next page, where the Spartans turn against the Minyans.</note>

And when they were to be put to death by the <term>executioners</term> <note>original: "manigoldi"; specifically those who carry out corporal or capital punishment</note>, the following night, according to the custom of the <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>the Spartans</note>, their wives, sorrowful and weeping, following a decision made by the husbands, took up this counsel; and having had the thought, they did not delay. Once evening fell, dressed in dark clothing, with their faces covered and bathed in tears, they went to the prisons to see their husbands. Permission was easily granted to them by the guards to go to the men, because they were <term>noblewomen</term> <note>original: "gentili donne"; implies high social standing and refined character</note>. 

When they arrived, time was not wasted in tears and lamentations; but immediately, having revealed their plan to their husbands, they exchanged clothes. They veiled the men in the manner of women, and the husbands—weeping and with eyes cast down to the ground, feigning <term>sorrow</term> <note>original: "tristizia"</note>—were aided by the darkness of the night and the respect shown to them as noblewomen. Deceiving the guards, they sent out those who were destined to die, while the women themselves remained in the place of the condemned. And the trick was not discovered until the executioners, going to put the condemned to death, found the wives in place of the husbands. 

And certainly, this was a great and singular love shown by these women. Some say that there is no hatred more deadly than that arising from the discords of wives, given that they are bound in an <term>indissoluble knot</term> <note>the lifelong bond of marriage</note> according to the ancient order of nature. And thus, when they are in accord with their husbands, their love surpasses all others; for, warmed by the fire of reason, it does not burn foolishly, but warms with pleasure and with such charity that they always "want and do not want" <note>this is an allusion to the classical definition of friendship: "to want and not want the same thing is firm friendship," often cited from the Roman historian Sallust</note> patiently. Love accustomed to such a pleasant unity leaves nothing undone that might hinder its preservation, and it performs no task lazily or coldly. If fortune is contrary, it takes on labors and dangers of its own will; with a <term>partner's solicitude</term> <note>original: "socia sollecitudine"; the diligent care shared between companions</note>, it considers and deliberates upon safety, finds remedies, and crafts deceptions, if the need requires it. # CHAPTER XXXVIII

## *Penelope, wife of Ulysses.*

**PENELOPE**, wife of Ulysses and daughter of King Icarius—a man of supreme prudence and virtue—was a woman of the greatest beauty and highest virtue <term>onestà</term> <note>original: "onestà," a term signifying moral integrity, chastity, and social honor</note>, and a most holy, eternal, and incorruptible example for women. The strength of her virtue was tested for a long time in vain; because when she was a young girl, a virgin, and much beloved for her beauty, her father married her to Ulysses, to whom she bore Telemachus. After this, he was sent—or rather, almost dragged by force—to the army at Troy; whereupon Penelope remained with Laertes her father-in-law, and Anticlea her mother-in-law, and with her young son. And certainly, as the war lasted for the space of ten years, she suffered no injury, except that she lived in the manner of a widow. But after Troy was destroyed, and as the Greek princes were returning home, rumors arrived that some of them had been endangered by sea storms among the rocks, some others had arrived in other lands, and some had been sunk in the sea,

### CHAPTER XL.

...to the reputation <note>This refers to the reputation of Sychaeus's hidden wealth mentioned on the previous page.</note>, Pygmalion, driven by greed and in the hope of possessing that treasure, treacherously murdered his brother-in-law, who was not on his guard. When Elissa learned of this, she bore the news with such agonizing grief that she barely restrained herself from taking her own life. After spending a long time in vain sorrow and weeping, frequently calling out the name of her beloved Sychaeus, and hurling every cruel curse against her brother, she resolved to flee. 

Whether she did this because of the guidance of a vision <note>This likely refers to the account in Virgil's Aeneid where the ghost of Sychaeus appears to Dido in a dream to reveal the murder and the location of the gold.</note>, as some say, or whether she did it by her own counsel—perhaps fearing that her brother's avarice might also lead her to her own death—she set aside the perceived weakness of a woman. 

She strengthened her spirit with <term>manly fortitude</term> <note>original: "fortezza d'uomo," a common trope in medieval literature praising women who displayed courage typically attributed to men.</note>. For this reason, she later earned the name "Dido" in the Phoenician language, which in the Latin tongue means "strong woman" <note>Historically, the name Dido is often associated with the Phoenician word for "wanderer," but the author here follows a tradition linking it to the concept of a "virago" or woman of great courage.</note>. 

Before doing anything else, she won over to her cause several of the leading men of the city, whom she knew hated Pygmalion for various reasons. ## CHAPTER XLV.

...a metal statue consecrated in her name; and she was numbered among the famous poets. And certainly the crowns of kings are no more famous than her crown, nor the mitres of priests, nor the laurels of those who triumph. And (if it is to be believed) just as she was happy *in her studies*, so *she was unhappy* in her falling in love; because, seized by love and occupied by an intolerable plague <note>original: "pestilenza," used here metaphorically to describe the overwhelming and destructive nature of obsessive love</note> for a young man; whether because of his charm, or his beauty, or some other reason, he was unwilling to consent to her desire. She, grieving over his stubborn beauty, composed verses against him; which I would have thought were <term>elegies</term> <note>A form of poetry traditionally used for laments or themes of love and loss</note>, because those are suited to such matters, if I had not read that she—as if scorning the forms of verse found by others in the past—invented a new generation of verses with certain "feet," which even now are named after her <note>This refers to the "Sapphic stanza," a specific rhythmic structure in classical poetry characterized by its unique "feet" or metrical units</note>. But what shall we say? Are the <term>Muses</term> <note>The nine Greek goddesses who presided over the arts and sciences</note> to be blamed? For when <term>Amphion</term> <note>In Greek mythology, a son of Zeus whose music was so powerful he could move stones to build the walls of Thebes</note> played, they were able to move the stones of the mountains; yet, while Sappho sang, they were not strong enough to soften the heart of a single youth.

## CHAPTER XLVI.

### *Roman Lucretia, wife of Collatinus.*

Lucretia the Roman, wife of Collatinus, was the guide of human chastity and a most holy name for ancient modesty. She was the daughter of Lucretius Spurius Tricipitinus, a very famous man among the Romans, and was the wife of Collatinus, who had been the brother <note>While historical tradition often identifies Tarquinius Collatinus as the nephew of the king, this text identifies him as a brother</note> of Tarquinius Priscus. It is uncertain whether she appeared more beautiful among other Roman women because of her physical beauty or her <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "onestà," which in this context refers specifically to moral and sexual integrity</note>.

## CHAPTER LI.

### *Hippo, a Greek Woman*

**Hippo** was a Greek woman, as is clearly seen in the books of the ancients; I can hardly believe she was valiant for only a single deed, for we climb to high things by degrees, and therefore no one suddenly reaches the summit. But since, through the malice of forgetfulness <note>original: "malignità di smenticanza" — a poetic way of describing how historical records and reputations are lost over time</note>, her lineage, her homeland, and other details have perished, I decided to make her story known so that what has reached us might not be lost, and that her due honor should not be taken from her. 

I say, then, that according to what we have found, this Hippo was by chance captured by enemy sailors. Since she was beautiful, and hearing that those who had captured her were conspiring against her and against her virtue <note>original: "onestà" — in this context, it specifically refers to her sexual integrity or reputation for chastity</note>, she valued the honor of her chastity so highly that, seeing no way to save it except through death, she did not wait to be violated <note>original: "sforzata" — literally "forced," a common historical euphemism for sexual assault</note>, but threw herself into the sea. In those waters she lost her life, and her virtue was saved. Who will not praise such a firm resolution?

# CHAPTER LII.

## *Megulia the Endowed.*

**MEGULIA,** whom the ancient Romans called **Dotata** <note>original: "Dotata" — meaning "the Dowered" or "the Endowed"</note>; was, I believe, a Roman woman living in that rough and—if I may call it so—holy age. In those times, those who sought the splendors of Asia and the riches of great kings had not yet left the embrace of poverty, that most excellent nurse <note>original: "nutricatrice" — a wet-nurse or nourisher; Boccaccio uses this to suggest that a simple, poor upbringing "nurtured" Roman virtue</note>; and by not despising poverty, they had not yet corrupted their noble souls (1). This woman acquired the surname **Dotata**, as I see it, more through the prominence of her family than by the merit of any particular deed of her own. For in those days, it seemed such a marvelous thing to provide a dowry of five hundred thousand denarii <term>denarii</term> <note>The denarius was a standard silver coin of the Roman Republic; in Boccaccio’s time, this sum represented an almost legendary amount of wealth for the early Roman period</note> that the name was bestowed upon the one to whom it was given. This name persisted for a long time, so much so that if, beyond the usual custom, anything was added to the dowry of any girl, she was immediately called by that name.

---

(1) <note>Cassino Manuscript: "who had tasted the noble act."</note>

<header>CHAPTER LII.</header>

### CHAPTER LII.

Megulia Dotata. O good simplicity! O praiseworthy poverty! That which poverty once made to seem like a truly marvelous thing would now, in our current decadence <note>original: "lascivia" — here referring to excessive luxury, indulgence, or a lack of moral restraint</note>, rightfully seem like a joke. For we have now so exceeded all measure in every respect that you will hardly find a <term>shoemaker</term> <note>original: "calzolaio"</note>, a <term>carpenter</term> <note>original: "marangone"</note>, or even a <term>porter</term> <note>original: "bastagio" — a manual laborer or carrier of burdens</note> or a peasant who is willing to take a wife for such a small sum or dowry. And this is no surprise, for even a common woman of the people has now adopted the crowns of queens, gold buckles, trimmings, and other ornaments; and they wear these things, I will not say with pride, but certainly without any shame. And I do not know whether to say that human spirits have grown so great by our yielding too much to them; or if rather—which I believe to be the absolute truth—it is through our own fault that vices and the insatiable desires of men have become so cherished (1).

---

**VETURIA**, a noble Roman woman, being already advanced in age, through her praiseworthy deeds brought her years to a praiseworthy vigor <note>original: "verdezza" — literally "greenness," used here to mean a flourishing or lasting reputation despite old age</note>. ### CHAPTER LIII.

What shall we say? The world belongs to women, and men have become womanish. # CHAPTER LIV.

## Thamaris the painter.

**Thamaris** <note>Also known as Timarete; she was a Greek painter known for her depiction of the goddess Artemis</note> was a noble painter in her time. Although antiquity has perhaps obscured much of her excellence, it has not yet been able to strip away her noble reputation or her artistry (1). It is said that during the ninetieth <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A period of four years used by the ancient Greeks to measure time; the 90th Olympiad occurred around 420 BCE</note>, she was the daughter of **Micon** the painter. Because we have read that at one time (2) there were two famous men named Micon in Athens, both of whom were painters, a distinction is made with only these few words: she was the daughter of that **Micon** who was given the nickname "the Younger." Certainly, whichever one was her father, she possessed such a marvelous intellect that, scorning the typical occupations of women, she followed her father’s craft. Thus, during the reign of **Archelaus** in Macedonia, she acquired great glory in the art of painting; so much so that...

Yet it did not come to pass that Artemisia saw this marvelous work completed, for she died before its end; nevertheless, the masters did not abandon the work upon the death of the Queen; rather, thinking...

# VIRGINIA, CHAPTER LVI.

Seeing that he who is a lord ought to have his eyes and his mind equally set upon humble speech, with grave and holy conduct, and above all to keep his hands clean from affairs with women, [such men] are not only lewd with their eyes, but with a furious mind they do not follow the judgment of the laws, but rather the counsel of scoundrels <note>original: "ruffiani"—referring here to procurers or those who facilitate illicit lust</note>. They become proud rather than humble, unless some little harlot commands it or softens them; and they not only receive gifts, but they demand them, engaging in trade and deception; and they even proceed to use force, inflamed with fury, if they cannot otherwise obtain what they desire. <header>IRENE, CHAPTER LVII.</header>

-># C H A P T E R  L V I I.<-

->## *Irene, daughter of Cratinus.*<-

It is not entirely certain whether <term>Irene</term> <note>Irene was an ancient Greek painter mentioned by Pliny the Elder.</note> was Greek, or in what period she flourished; nevertheless, it was believed that she was Greek because it is clear that she was the daughter of a <term>painter</term> <note>original: "pintore"</note> named <term>Cratinus</term>, and was his pupil in the art. In this art, I think she is as worthy of praiseworthy words as she surpassed her master in skill and fame (1); her renown still endures in many things, while the father is not mentioned except because of her. ### CHAPTER LXII.

#### *Flora, a Roman courtesan.*

**THE** ancients seem to prove that Flora was a Roman woman, from whom favorable fortune added as much in fame as her shameful gain took away from her reputation. And she, as every man confirms, was a very wealthy woman; but there is disagreement as to how she acquired those riches; for some say that she spent the entire flower of her youth...

Which virtue certainly, if we wish to look with a clearer eye, consists not only in refraining from the touch of strange men—something which many do only by force—but it is necessary that the woman, so that she may be held entirely virtuous before all others, restrain her greedy and wandering eyes, and that she constrain them within her own boundaries; her words should be few and honest, and she should speak only at the proper time; she must flee idleness as the most certain and most deadly enemy of virtue; she must abstain from excessive eating and *drinking*, for unchastity <note>original: "disonestà"</note> is fueled by food and wine; she must shun singing and dancing as the arrows of unchastity; *dedicate herself to temperance and sobriety*; take care of the affairs of her house; keep her eyes closed to dishonest conversations; refuse ointments and perfumes <note>In this period, heavy scents and oils were often viewed as signs of vanity or tools of seduction.</note>; refuse excessive ornaments; trample underfoot evil thoughts and appetites, and with all her strength oversee and keep watch over holy thoughts: and so that I do not *pass over* every testimony—

It is difficult to determine who possessed the greater faith: the one who died first, or the one who survived her. The devotion of the former made her virtue eternal, while the devotion of the latter made her name immortal.

# CHAPTER LXIX.

## Theoxena of Thessaly.

**THEOXENA** <note>Theoxena was a noblewoman from Thessaly whose story is recorded by the Roman historian Livy; Boccaccio uses her as an example of tragic maternal devotion.</note> of Thessaly was a woman of noble birth, who left to those who follow a glorious testimony of herself: on one hand for her sweet piety, and on the other for her resolute violence <note>original: "costante atrocità"; here meaning a terrifying or shocking steadfastness in her final actions.</note>. She was the daughter of Herodicus, a prince of Thessaly, during the time when Philip <note>Philip V of Macedon (r. 221–179 BC).</note>, the son of Demetrius, reigned in Macedonia. She had a half-sister on her father's side named Archo. After their father had first died through the malice of that same Philip, in the course of time—his wickedness having grown—that same king killed the husbands of these sisters, leaving each of them with one son from her husband. Therefore, these women being widows, Archo first remarried a prince of her own people named Poris, and by him she had many children; but Theoxena, though sought as a wife by many princes in vain, remained a widow for a longer time with a more resolute spirit. But after Archo had died, [Theoxena] having compassion for her nephews so that they would not fall <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page; the story continues with her marrying her sister's widower to protect the children.</note>—

# CHAPTER LXX.

### *Berenice, Queen of Cappadocia.*

**Berenice** of Pontus, who was also called Laodice <note>original: "Leodice"; historical records usually refer to her as Laodice, the sister of Mithridates the Great</note>, although she may seem to hold a place among famous women because of the nobility of her birth, it is judged that she much more deserved it—not just for the warm love of her son, with which most mothers are inflamed—but for the merit of her marvelous boldness in taking revenge for him. She was the daughter of that *Mithridates* <note>Mithridates V Euergetes</note>, King of Pontus, who had waged war alongside the Romans against *Aristonicus* <note>A pretender to the throne of Pergamum who led a revolt against Rome</note>, and who died shortly thereafter of a sudden death; she was also the sister of *Mithridates* <note>Mithridates VI, known as "the Great," one of Rome's most formidable enemies</note>, the son of the elder Mithridates and an enemy of the Romans through a long war. She was the wife of King *Ariarathes* <note>Ariarathes VI</note> of Cappadocia, by whom she had two sons. This king was killed by *Cordius* through a betrayal orchestrated by Mithridates, Berenice's own brother. ### CHAPTER LXXI.

Who would say that this woman was not only Roman, but rather of the school of Lucretia <note>Lucretia was a legendary Roman noblewoman whose suicide after being raped led to the establishment of the Roman Republic; she became the ultimate symbol of female virtue</note> rather than a barbarian? Still present before her was the prison, and the chains of the victors clattered around her; and over her head were prepared the axes <term>mannaje: heavy blades or cleavers used for executions</term> of the harsh punisher; and it was not enough for that woman that her liberty had been restored to her; because the indignation over her defiled body had driven her honorable heart with such great force, that the spirited woman—the avenger of that wicked deed—did not fear, had it been necessary, being led away captive in chains, entering prison, and submitting her head to the axes, so long as she, with a firm command, could induce her servants to put that wicked adulterer <note>original: "adultero," used here to describe the centurion who had violated her</note> to death. 

Where will you find a harsher man, a more spirited captain, or a more steadfast commander against those who have behaved wickedly? Where will you hear of a more sagacious or more daring woman, or a more diligent guardian of a woman’s honor <note>original: "onestade"</note>? This woman saw, with a marvelous sharpness of mind, that it is better to go to a certain death than to return to her husband's house with uncertain honor; for she could not prove, except with great danger, that her mind had remained chaste within her violated body. # CHAPTER LXXVI.

## *Hypsicratea, Queen of Pontus.*

**Hypsicratea**, although her lineage is not known, was nonetheless the wife of the great Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI, known as "the Great," was the King of Pontus and one of the Roman Republic's most formidable enemies</note>, and a great queen of Pontus <note>An ancient kingdom on the southern coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Turkey</note>. She was of marvelous beauty and possessed an invincible love for her husband; she is so worthy of praise that, because of that devotion, she earned perpetual glory for her name. 

While Mithridates was engaged in a long and costly war with the Romans—and although he, according to barbarian custom <note>The author refers to the practice of polygamy or having multiple concubines, which Greek and Roman writers often labeled as "barbarian" behavior</note>, had other wives and mistresses—she, inflamed by the greatest love, was always his most faithful and inseparable companion, whether he went into battle or prepared his military forces. 

Certainly, finding his absence painful and believing that no one could serve him better, and wanting to ensure that the majority of those tending to him were not strangers, she resolved to follow him, even though she knew it would be a great hardship, so that she might personally perform all necessary tasks for the husband she loved so deeply. Despite the fact that she had tirelessly provided so much aid to his life, he did this so that she might not outlive him. 

And certainly, the ungrateful deed of Mithridates could not diminish the deserved glory of Hypsicratea. Her body, which was mortal, was dispatched to death before its time by poison; but her name has reached us, and will live perpetually in glorious fame through the testimony of venerable writers, and it could not be overwhelmed by any future length of time.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.

### *Julia, daughter of Gaius Julius Caesar.*

**JULIA** was perhaps the most famous woman in the entire world, both because of her **lineage** <term>schiatta: a noble family line or ancestry</term> and her husband; but she was even more famous for her most holy love and for her sudden death. She was the only daughter of Julius Caesar, born to Cornelia his wife, who was the daughter of Cinna, a man who had been consul four times. This Julius traced his origins through many kings and other descendants back to **Aeneas** <note>In Roman mythology, Aeneas was a Trojan hero and the legendary ancestor of the Roman people; Caesar’s family, the Julii, claimed direct descent from his son, Iulus.</note>, leader of the Trojans, on his father's side <margin>The Cassinese Codex reads: "of the Trojans." The Latin text reads: "traced his paternal origin."</margin>, and on his mother’s side from **Ancus Marcius** <note>The fourth King of Rome, credited with expanding the city and founding the port of Ostia.</note>, who had previously been King of the Romans; and he was greatly honored with glories, battles, triumphs, and a **perpetual dictatorship** <term>dittatura: a Roman political office granting absolute power, which Caesar eventually held for life.</term>. Later, she became the wife of Pompey the Great, a man most famous among the Romans at that time, who for a long period exhausted not only the earth but the heavens, conquering kings, casting them down and appointing them anew, subjugating nations, and hunting down **pirates** <term>corsari: specifically the Cilician pirates who had dominated the Mediterranean until Pompey defeated them in 67 BCE.</term>,

### Epicharis the servant.

**Epicharis the servant** <note>original: "Epitare serva"; referring to the historical Epicharis, a key figure in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero</note>, was believed to be a foreign woman rather than a **Roman**; and not only was she not famous because she was not of **noble lineage** <term>nobile schiatta</term>, but even worse, as the daughter of a slave, she was a **freedwoman** <term>libertina</term> <note>a former slave who had been granted legal freedom</note>. [Ne]ro, she was put to death, and **Poppaea** was joined in marriage to **Caesar** <note>the Emperor Nero</note>. Nero did not want her body to be burned according to the custom of the **Romans**, but he willed that she be buried in the manner of foreign kings with a burial of great pomp; having her carried publicly, and with many fragrant spices, he willed that she be placed in the tomb of the **Julii** <note>the Mausoleum of Augustus, the dynastic tomb of the Julio-Claudian emperors</note>. And in the council he praised her—and especially her wondrous beauty—with a long and ornate oration, attributing to her certain gifts of fortune and nature with which she was adorned, in place of more famous virtues. 

I had much to say, among these fortunes of **Poppaea**, against her excessive softness, flatteries, lasciviousness, and tears, which are the most certain and deadly poison of women to the minds of those who believe them; but I have decided to leave these things out, so that I do not seem to be writing a **satire** rather than a **history** (1).

# CHAPTER LXXXIV.

## *Triaria.*

**Triaria** was a woman not known for any other splendor of her lineage, except for the fact that she was the wife of Lucius Vitellius, Emperor of Rome <note>Boccaccio here refers to Lucius Vitellius as the Emperor, though historical records usually identify his brother Aulus as the Emperor and Lucius as a powerful general and brother who shared in his authority</note>. Because of her fervent love toward her husband, and because she had a soul naturally inclined toward cruelty, she possessed such ferocity that, contrary to the custom of women, she is deemed worthy of being remembered. 

Therefore, while the Emperor Vitellius and Vespasian <note>The future Emperor Vespasian, who was then leading a rebellion to seize the throne</note> were in discord over the empire, it happened that Lucius entered that land <note>Terracina</note> by night. ### *Joan the Englishwoman.* <note>original: "Giovanni Anglica"</note>

**JOAN**, although she appeared to be a man by name, was nonetheless a woman in fact; her unheard-of audacity made her known to the whole world, and she has been widely discussed ever since. ## *Irene of Athens.*

**IRENE** was a most noble woman of Athens, and was famous for her singular beauty; after the Emperor Constantine <note>Constantine V, reigned 741–775 AD</note> had her brought from her home to Constantinople, he gave her as a wife to his son Leo <note>Leo IV, known as "the Khazar"</note>. # CHAPTER 101.

## Constance, Queen of Sicily.

**Constance, the Roman Empress,** was famous throughout the land for reaching the highest pinnacle of worldly status; but because she shared this common honor with many others, it seems to have diminished the admiration of those who look back upon her. Those who wish to stand out in our own age must seek another cause for their excellence <note>original: "eccellenza"</note>, and such a cause was certainly not lacking in this woman. Indeed, even if fame had not been granted to her for any other merit, she became celebrated at least for the sake of her son alone <note>Her son was the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, known as "Stupor Mundi" or the Wonder of the World</note>. She was the daughter of William, the excellent King of Sicily <note>Historical records usually identify Constance as the daughter of Roger II and aunt/sister of the Williams; the text here follows a different traditional genealogy</note>. It is said by many that at the time of her birth, Joachim, the Calabrian abbot <term>abate Calavrese</term> <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), a famous mystic and theologian known for his prophetic visions</note>, who was gifted with a prophetic spirit, told William that the daughter—

In the kingdom of Tancred, and after him during the reign of his son William—who was still a young boy—it happened that, either due to the unworthy succession of kings or the schemes of the Barons, wars broke out on every side. The kingdom seemed to be heading toward utter destruction by sword and fire. Because of this, some who felt compassion for these misfortunes recalled what was to follow: namely, that Constance should be given as a wife to a certain prince, so that through his power and efforts, this deadly upheaval might be prevented.

And it was not achieved without deception and great toil—even with the Pope’s consent—to get Constance to agree to such a proposal. She remained firm in the purpose of her religious vows <term>professione</term> <note>Her "profession" refers to the formal solemn vows she took when entering the convent, which were intended to be lifelong.</note> and appeared to resist the change. 

But despite her resistance, and because the situation had already progressed to a point where she could not easily withdraw, she was given as a wife to Henry <note>Henry VI (1165–1197), known here as Arrigo, was the son of Frederick Barbarossa.</note>, Emperor of the Romans, son of Frederick I.

Thus, while he was in prison, nearly without hope of freedom and kept in irons, it happened that he came to the mind of **Camiola** <note>Camiola Turinga, a wealthy and famously virtuous widow from Messina.</note>. Seeing him despised by his own brothers, she felt compassion for his misfortune. She deliberated within herself whether she could honorably seek to restore him to liberty; seeing no other way to safeguard her <term>reputation</term> <note>original: "onestà"; in this period, a woman of high standing could not financialy support or ransom a man without a formal social tie, such as marriage, without risking her moral reputation.</note> than by taking him as her husband, she secretly sent someone to ask if he wished to leave prison by that means. This was easily obtained; and so, with every legal solemnity observed, he married her as his wife by pro- <note>The text breaks here; the full word is likely "promessa" (promise) or "procura" (proxy), indicating a legal marriage contract signed while he was still in captivity.</note>

## CHAPTER CII.

...the <term>guardian</term> <note>original: "curatore"; likely a legal representative or overseer for Orlando’s affairs while he was a prisoner of war.</note> consenting to it, and under the security of the ring. And without delay, Camiola sent two thousand <term>ounces of silver</term> <note>A massive fortune; in 14th-century Sicily, the "once d'argento" was a standard unit of account for significant wealth.</note>, and once it was paid, he returned free from prison; yet he did not go to the house of his bride any differently than if not a single word had been spoken of the matter.

Camiola was at first filled with wonder; and finally, sensing the ingratitude of that man, she became indignant. Then, so that it would not appear she was moved by anger more than by reason, she kindly sent a request that he should complete the nuptials. But since he denied that he had anything to do with her, she had him summoned before the **ecclesiastical judge**, and with authentic documents and the testimony of worthy men, she proved that he was indeed her husband.

When this was done, he confessed out of shame; and once the kindness this woman had shown toward him became known, he was rebuked by his brothers and urged by his friends. He was thus induced to consent to the woman’s demand, and he himself asked to perform the wedding. 

But that woman of great spirit spoke nearly these words in the presence of many: "Orlando, I have cause to thank God, because before you could corrupt the integrity of my virtue under this pretext of marriage, you have shown the wickedness of your... <note>The sentence concludes on the following page, where Camiola famously rejects him despite having won the legal right to the marriage.</note>

## CHAPTER CIII.

### *Joan, Queen of Jerusalem.*

**JOAN**, Queen of Jerusalem and Sicily <note>Joan I of Naples (reigned 1343–1382), who held the titles of Queen of Naples, Jerusalem, and Sicily</note>, is famous beyond all other women of our time for her lineage, her power, and her character: it seemed it would be a hateful thing if I had remained silent about her; and yet to be silent about her would be better than to write so little of her in vain. This woman, then, was the first daughter of Charles, the glorious Duke of Calabria <note>Charles of Anjou, Duke of Calabria (1298–1328)</note>, the firstborn of Robert of famous memory, King of Sicily and Jerusalem, and of Mary <note>Marie of Valois</note>, sister of Philip, King of France; of whose father and mother (1) if we wish to seek the grandfathers and great-grandfathers, we shall not cease until, through the royal ancestors, we come to Dardanus, the first founder of Ilion <note>Troy</note>, whom the ancients said was the son of Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods</note>. Attend with prudence; do not judge by outward appearances <note>A reference to John 7:24: "Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."</note>, but give just judgments, keeping in your soul—and always fearing—the eternal judgment of God.

# EDITOR'S NOTES

---

(A) Upon reading these maxims, the reader will find it difficult to believe they were written by that same Boccaccio who indulged in such a rush of indecency within the pages of the **Decameron**. But let us consider the moral change in the life of Messer Francesco <note>Original: "M. Francesco." This appears to be an error by the editor or a misprint in the original text; the author of the *Decameron* is Giovanni Boccaccio. The editor may have momentarily confused him with his friend Francesco Petrarch.</note>, and every doubt will be removed; indeed, we shall take it as proof that he wrote the **Book of Famous Women** <note>Original: "Libro delle Donne Illustri," referring to Boccaccio's Latin work *De mulieribus claris*.</note> after 1362, the year in which his mind was restored to a purer state by Father Gioacchino Ciani, a Carthusian. Boccaccio used to spend his days as a person concerned only with the present, giving free rein to his lust; by depicting the varied nature of men in various conditions of life in the **Decameron**, he dispensed to others that poison with which he had corrupted his own mind and heart. When the Blessed Petroni <note>Pietro Petroni (1311–1361), a Carthusian monk from Siena known for his piety. On his deathbed, he reportedly had a vision that led him to send a message to Boccaccio urging him to repent.</note>, a Carthusian and a man entirely of God, was near death, as if comforted by a divine will, he sent for Messer Boccaccio through his fellow brother, Father Gioacchino Ciani, so that he might pull him out of that swamp of vice. # EDITOR'S NOTES

the good friar <note>Father Gioacchino Ciani, who delivered a deathbed warning from the holy man Pietro Petroni to Boccaccio.</note> stood before Boccaccio and, assuming the manner of a person sent by God, said to him: that a near and miserable end hung over him if he did not cease his shameful behaviors and stop leading others into lust with his writings. As the friar spoke these and similar things, Master Boccaccio was seized by a great terror; and he so firmly set his mind on the plan of giving himself to God that he might perhaps have finished his days in some convent, had his friend Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous poet and scholar, wrote a well-known letter to Boccaccio advising him not to abandon his studies or burn his books out of religious fear.</note> not dissuaded him. If, therefore, in these *Lives*, O reader, you see Boccaccio providing moral lessons different from those of the **Decameron**, consider him a convert, and assume that this Book was written after 1362, the year in which the author’s mind changed, and he also changed his style of writing.

I come now to the evidence. Although scholars are in disagreement, the *Chronicle of Marianus Scotus* <note>Marianus Scotus (1028–1082) was an Irish monk and chronicler whose Universal Chronicle was widely influential in the Middle Ages.</note> is the oldest book in which one reads of Pope Joan, and these are its words: *Pope Leo died on the Kalends of August. Joan succeeded him for two years, five months, and four days.* <note>original: "Leo Papa obiit Kalendis Augusti. Huic successit Joanna annis duobus, mensibus quinque, diebus quatuor."</note> Scotus was born in the year 1028 and died in the year '86 of the same century, 236 years after the election of Benedict III; therefore, about two and a half centuries separated him from the reported event. He is not a contemporary writer; and since he is not, let us see if he received such a fine tale from writers of that same time. Among these, greater faith should be granted to the one who lived not only in the same century, but in the same year and in the same place where the event occurred: this is <term>Anastasius the Librarian</term> <note>Anastasius Bibliothecarius (c. 810–879), a high-ranking cleric and historian in Rome often credited with the "Liber Pontificalis."</note>, who, as an eyewitness in Rome of the death of Leo IV and the immediate elevation of Benedict III, makes no mention of any sort of Joan who, between these two pontiffs, held the highest authority over Christian affairs. Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, William, Librarian of the Holy Roman Church, the Frankish Annals known as the *Bertinian Annals* <note>The *Annales Bertiniani*, a primary source for 9th-century Frankish history.</note>, Regino, Abbot of Prüm, and Hincmar of Reims—all of whom lived in the ninth century—remained silent about this "Popess," and their silence is a powerful argument to clarify for us the falsity of Scotus's account. Indeed, it cannot enter into a reasonable mind that these men came to a common agreement...
