In the copies of <term>Anastasius</term> <note>Anastasius the Librarian (c. 810–879), the purported author of the *Liber Pontificalis*.</note>, he noticed the words *as it is asserted, as it is said* <note>original: "ut asseritur, ut dicitur"</note>, which the Roman Librarian used in the narrative of the female Pope; and he concludes quite rightly that this manner of recounting is not a description of a significant event seen with one’s own eyes, but rather a tale truly picked up at the crossroads <note>original: "al trivio," referring to common gossip or street-corner rumors.</note>. This single observation by <term>Sarrau</term> <note>Claude Sarrau (1600–1651), a French scholar who corresponded with other great thinkers of his time regarding historical forgeries.</note>, which swiftly uncovers the fraud of the impostor who thrust this fable into the chronicle of Anastasius, relieves us of the obligation to go on at any greater length. 

But why do we lead you deeper into this, reader? Very weighty reasons—which you can find in the works of <term>Labbe</term> <note>Philippe Labbe (1607–1667), a Jesuit scholar known for his work on the history of Church Councils.</note>, in <term>Natale Alessandro</term> <note>Noël Alexandre (1639–1724), a Dominican theologian and church historian.</note>, in <term>Allacci</term> <note>Leo Allatius (1586–1669), a scholar and librarian of the Vatican.</note>, and in a hundred other extraordinary writers, and which we omit for the sake of brevity—very strongly guarantee our opinion against any opposition; for neither <term>Marianus Scotus</term> <note>An 11th-century chronicler whose work was frequently cited in the Pope Joan debate.</note> nor <term>Martinus Polonus</term> <note>Martin of Opava (d. 1278), a Dominican chronicler whose popular history was later altered by others to include the Pope Joan story.</note> left the story of Joan written in their chronicles, but it was placed there by force by a corrupting hand.

We believe that the question is clarified by this very brief argument; if our words do not suit the <term>heretics</term> <note>A term used here by the editor to refer to Protestant polemicists who used the Pope Joan story to attack the papacy.</note> in particular, and they love to fight a battle that is already over, we shall step aside, and the Protestant <term>Blondel</term> <note>David Blondel (1591–1655), a French Protestant clergyman who famously published a treatise proving the story of Pope Joan was a myth, much to the chagrin of his fellow Protestants.</note> alone will hold our ground. (F) A letter written by the **Great Turk**, **Mehmed II** <note>Mehmed the Conqueror (1432–1481), the Ottoman Sultan who captured Constantinople in 1453.</note>, to **Pope Nicholas V**, and the reply from the latter to that Conqueror, are historical monuments which, it seems to me, have not yet come to the notice of anyone. It is truly astonishing that <term>Baronius</term> <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), an influential Cardinal and historian known for his multi-volume *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note>, who wrote extensively on the actions taken by Nicholas regarding the immense growth of Turkish power, then remained silent about these two letters, which should certainly be regarded as of no small significance. ...his Imperial Library <note>The "Biblioteca Cesarea" or Imperial Library of the Holy Roman Empire in Vienna.</note>, also makes mention of a letter from the Emperor of the Turks <note>The Sultan.</note> translated into the German tongue; and perhaps it will not be different from this one which we now bring to light.

The Greek Empire <note>Often referred to today as the Byzantine Empire.</note>, founded upon the ruins of that of Rome, was born staggering, and in the course of the 1,123 years it remained standing, it faced the greatest perils both from the external aggressions of the Barbarians and from internal discords, as well as from weak rulers who turned their minds more to theological trifles than to the management of state affairs. Among the Barbarians with whom the Greeks sustained the fiercest struggle were the Turks. The religious opinions preached by that notorious impostor Muhammad <note>The author uses "solenne impostore," reflecting the typical 18th and 19th-century European perspectives on Islam.</note> had, in a certain way, changed the condition of the Arab mind: a paradise of carnal delights promised to those dying in battle rendered men exceedingly ardent in combat, and despisers—if not seekers—of death; and therefore their power at its birth was like a torrent which, by a sudden flood, grew, overflowed, and devastated.

In the eleventh century, the Turks emerged from the gorges of the Caucasus and, falling upon Persia—which had been weakened by long wars with the lords of Constantinople—they placed it under their yoke and threatened the very seat of the Greek Empire with ruin. Under the reign of Constantine Doukas <note>Constantine X Doukas, Byzantine Emperor from 1059 to 1067.</note> in the eleventh century, they threw the states of Greece into turmoil. The brave Romanus Diogenes <note>Romanus IV Diogenes, who reigned from 1068 to 1071; he is famous for his defeat at the Battle of Manzikert.</note> had blunted their pride in many battles, but final- <margin>Catchword: final-</margin>

...miserably defeated, was captured and blinded <note>The author refers to the aftermath of the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, where the Byzantine Emperor Romanus IV Diogenes was defeated by the Seljuk Turks.</note>. The subsequent rise and fall of princes on the throne of Constantine—to which they ascended through crime and from which they were dragged by crime—left the reins of government wavering for a long time, and added boldness to the enemy. Alexios Komnenos saw the islands of Chios, Lesbos, Rhodes, and Samos snatched away by the Turks; under Andronicus in the 14th century, in the heart of the empire, the Turks extended their dominion over all of Asia Minor, which, divided into seven governments, recognized the Ottoman as its lord; and finally under John Palaeologus in 1372, Murad <note>original: "Amurat"</note> pushed his conquests into Thrace, took Adrianople <note>Modern-day Edirne, Turkey.</note>, and designated that city as the capital of his empire. The Turks had been witnesses to the great wealth that enriched the Greek throne back when they were brought there by Nikephoros Botaneiates to take the crown from Michael VII Doukas <note>A reference to the civil wars of the 11th century where Byzantine factions hired Turkish mercenaries, inadvertently showing them the empire's vulnerabilities.</note>; now that they saw that throne within their reach, they began more than ever to plot its conquest. Their designs were favored not a little by the weakening of the empire, which had been previously dismembered into two other empires—namely, those of Trebizond and Adrianople—while the Latins <note>Western European crusaders who established the Latin Empire (1204–1261) after the Fourth Crusade.</note> held supreme power in Constantinople.

Mehmed possessed a conqueror's soul within a very robust frame, along with all the vices and virtues that are never separated from such a spirit. In 1453, he laid a fierce siege to Constantinople, and only when the brave Giustiniani <note>Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, a Genoese captain who led the defense of the city</note> was removed from the walls due to his wounds did the Sultan take it by assault; it was as if the breast of an Italian were the greatest bulwark of the dying Roman Empire <note>The Byzantine Empire was the direct successor to the Roman Empire; contemporaries often referred to it as the "Empire of the Romans."</note>.

The fall of the Greek Empire struck great fear into the hearts of the Italian powers, but it did not turn them toward a better disposition. Nicholas V, then Pope, for whom the news of this conquest was bitter, did not stand idly by <note>original: "mani alla cintola" — literally "with hands at the belt," an idiom for being unproductive</note> as if it were merely a spectacle to watch and nothing more. He, who since 1451 had sent Cardinal Cusa <note>Nicholas of Cusa, a famous philosopher and diplomat</note> to Germany <note>original: "Alemagna"</note> to harmonize minds and spur them to war against the Turk; to France, Cardinal Estouteville; and to England, the Archbishop of Ravenna, Orsini, to reconcile and restore peace between these two warring kingdoms <note>A reference to the final stages of the Hundred Years' War</note>, now more than ever made his voice heard from the Chair of Saint Peter. But Italy was boiling and in discord. Ferdinand, King of Naples, was at war with Florence; Venice with Milan; the Fregosi and Adorni families, with internal discords, were bringing Genoa to a bad state; France with Brittany... but why do I speak of those beyond the Alps? Italy alone, in that virile age of hers, was sufficient for the common salvation; but—

The aforementioned Bull seems to be the one that begins: "Long ago, there was a most bitter enemy of Christ’s Church, a most cruel persecutor, Muhammad, the son of Satan, etc." <note>original Latin: "Fuit jam olim Ecclesiæ Christi hostis acerrimus, crudelissimus persecutor Mahometes, filius Satanæ, ecc."</note>, in which the Pope, having likened Muhammad to the dragon seen by St. John <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Revelation 12:4, where a great red dragon sweeps a third of the stars from the sky with its tail</note> who with one blow of his tail dragged a third of the stars to the earth; and after having described the iniquities in which the Turk <note>Referring to the Ottoman Sultan, Mehmed II, and his forces</note> indulged during the capture of Constantinople, and his design to extend his dominion into the West, he attempted to encourage the Christian princes, stirring their minds with holy exhortations toward a Crusade <term>Crociata</term> <note>A religiously sanctioned military campaign aimed at reclaiming formerly Christian territories</note>, and promising payment in ready and ringing cash, for which the armies would have been supplied by tithes to be paid not only by the Clergy, but by the Cardinals, and even by himself.

For, as it is easy for readers to discern, the Turk <note>Referring to Sultan Mehmed II</note>—after prefixing all those titles in which Turkish arrogance was so generous—makes a very great <term>boast</term> <note>original: "jattanza" — a term for boastful pride or arrogance, often associated with military bravado</note> of his rights to the city of Rome and of his forces, and says something of his probable conversion to the faith of Christ. Pope Nicholas did not show himself at all terrified by the Turk’s letter, but through a confidence in his own forces and those of the Christian Princes, he used a style of writing that should have made it clear to the Conqueror that he awaited him with a firm footing. And since as a prince he gave proof of firmness, as the father of the faithful he turned lovingly toward Mehmed to bring him back to the path of truth.

# THE GOOD USE
# OF LOGIC
## IN MATTERS OF RELIGION
### WORK OF CANON
## ALFONSO MUZZARELLI
### EIGHT VOLUMES
->Price: 27.60 Austrian lire; 24.00 Italian lire<-

I have always preferred to occupy my printing presses <note>The Italian "tipi" literally means "types," referring to the movable type used in the printing process.</note> with editions of distinguished works already established by public approval, rather than with the transient writings of the day, which are but a vain pasture for superficial and light reading. Among these, I have now chosen to reprint the most useful and most acclaimed work of the celebrated canon *Alfonso Muzzarelli* <note>Alfonso Muzzarelli (1749–1813) was a Jesuit theologian and a leading figure in the "Counter-Enlightenment," dedicated to defending Catholic doctrine against secular philosophy.</note>, who was born in Ferrara and died in Paris in 1815, titled *The Good Use of Logic in Matters of Religion.*

This is a collection of many dissertations on various subjects concerning Religion and the Catholic Church—specifically those most contested or misunderstood by modern Philosophy <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to the Enlightenment movement, which the author views as being prone to its own form of dogmatic prejudice.</note>. This misunderstanding arises not because these subjects are actually opposed to the true enlightenment and the just observations of philosophy itself, but because they are viewed without a precision of principles and with an eye clouded by too many prejudices; for it must be confessed that philosophy itself possesses its own great and most fatal prejudices. In these times, the illusion of certain maxims is so great that many, even among the virtuous, allow themselves to be ensnared by the insidious observations and the unfaithful declamations of the enemies of Religion. This occurs particularly regarding certain points of history or ecclesiastical doctrine, which are represented as being contrary to, or less in harmony with, the truth and the spirit of the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>; however, when these points are better considered and studied with correct principles and sincere facts, they are found to be in perfect agreement with the truth and with the most essential attributes of the Church. Study and...

--- Page 508 ---
<meta>This page continues the publisher’s preface from the previous page, detailing the virtues of Canon Alfonso Muzzarelli’s theological defense against Enlightenment philosophy. It concludes with the publisher's signature and the bibliographical history of the edition.</meta>

good faith heal many who are infirm: this is the medicine that the celebrated Canon *Mazzarelli* <note>Alfonso Muzzarelli (1749–1813) was a Jesuit theologian and a leading figure in the "Counter-Enlightenment," dedicated to defending Catholic doctrine against secular philosophy.</note> knew how to prepare in his celebrated work. Being deeply versed in all matters of sacred science <note>Sacred science refers to theology and the study of scripture.</note>, he has represented things in their true light; and by clearing away—through theology, history, and the most exquisite reasoning of a sincere philosophy—all the clouds of error and bad faith, he leads the reader back to the true and wise way of seeing and thinking about matters of Religion.

The present work can never be recommended enough to priests, who need to know and to make known to others the doctrines most contested in our times, and most useful for strengthening the true spirit of a reasoned Christianity. Even laypeople <note>The Italian "secolari" (seculars) refers to those who are not members of the clergy.</note> will find here delightful and erudite reading due to the variety and correctness of the discussions, as well as the easy manner of handling the most delicate and important topics. Oh, if only this were read with some attention by the many in our day who wish to pass judgment and write on the matters of a Religion they do not know; by the many who find nothing but abuses and errors, ignorance or fanaticism, in the doctrines or practices of the Catholic Church; I do not doubt that they would soon strip away their prejudices to confess that things studied at the sources of truth are quite different from how they appear when disfigured by a lack of proper study, or by the malice of a lying history and a reckless rationalism <note>Rationalism, in this context, refers to the 18th-century philosophical trend that prioritized human reason over divine revelation, often viewed by the Church as a threat to faith.</note>.

This work, in fact, having been providently reprinted and distributed in the early years of the century, produced excellent effects and corrected the public spirit on many important ecclesiastical matters. It has been translated into French and Spanish, as well as into Latin in Hungary. Our most reputable journals, both local and foreign, have given it the highest praise.

The present edition was based on the fifth Florence edition of 1821, which itself was based on the fourth Rome edition, completed with all the Author’s additions.
**Giovanni Silvestri.** <note>Giovanni Silvestri (1796–1855) was a prominent Milanese printer and publisher known for his "Biblioteca Scelta" (Selected Library) collection.</note>

->*THE PRINTER*<-

Both Letters from two very distinguished Personages, which precede a work so worthily crafted and discussed by our Author, as well as the mention of it in the *Italian Library* <note>The *Biblioteca Italiana* was an influential literary and scientific journal published in Milan; it served as a major platform for intellectual debate in the 19th century.</note> in No. CLXXXVI, month of June, 1831, on page 399, excuse me from having to search for further authoritative testimonies to demonstrate to the reader that this is a work of the highest value and has been long desired. It is a work that must at once reassure even the most delicate conscience regarding the kind of Usury <term>Usury (Italian: *usura*): In historical Catholic theology, "usury" referred to any interest charged on a loan. Mastrofini sought to redefine this, arguing that moderate interest was permissible in a modern economy, provided it did not exploit the poor.</term> which is treated herein.
